title: Psoriasis
summary: Sharply defined, scaly plaques caused by IL-23/IL-17 inflammation. Manage with topical steroid and vitamin D, steroid breaks, and screening for joints and comorbidities.

hero.alt: AI illustration of silvery-scaled psoriasis plaques on elbows and knees

glance.think: Well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees, scalp or lower back; nail pitting.
glance.engine: IL-23/Th17/IL-17 inflammation driving very fast keratinocyte turnover (3–5 days instead of about a month).
glance.backbone: Emollient plus potent steroid and vitamin D analogue, with planned steroid breaks.
glance.never_miss: Erythroderma or generalised pustular psoriasis (same day), and joint symptoms suggesting psoriatic arthritis.

what: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease that relapses and remits. It affects roughly **1–3%** of the UK population. Onset peaks in young adulthood and again in mid-life, and about a third of patients have a family history.
It can involve the nails and joints (**psoriatic arthritis**). It is associated with metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease and depression.

what.title: Main types
what.text: Chronic plaque (most common, about 80–90%), guttate, flexural (inverse), scalp, palmoplantar and nail. Erythrodermic and generalised pustular psoriasis are rare emergencies.

figure.caption: Psoriasis pathogenesis: immune activation (IL-23/IL-17, TNF-α) drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation, giving a turnover of 3–5 days instead of about 28 days and producing thick scaly plaques.

list: **Genetic predisposition** (e.g. HLA-C*06:02, linked with early-onset and guttate disease) plus immune activation.
Key cytokine axis: **IL-23 → Th17 → IL-17**, plus TNF-α, causing keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inflammation.
Very fast epidermal turnover produces thick, scaly plaques.
Trauma, scratches and surgery: the **Koebner phenomenon**
Drugs: lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, and abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids
HIV, which can cause severe or atypical disease

head: Type
What you see
Where
rows: Sharply demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale; pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed (Auspitz sign)
Shiny, well-defined, moist, little or no scale; may be colonised by Candida
Axillae, groin, natal cleft, under the breasts
Many small ‘raindrop’ plaques, often 2–3 weeks after a strep throat
Thick adherent scale, often extending beyond the hairline
Pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discolouration, subungual hyperkeratosis

features: Itch is usually mild to moderate but can be severe. Fissures on the palms and soles are painful. **Nail disease is a clue to a higher risk of psoriatic arthritis.**

features.title: Skin of colour
features.text: Scale may be thicker and erythema harder to see, often looking violaceous or grey. Post-inflammatory pigment change is marked and can last longer than the plaques.

list: **Assess:** body surface area (BSA), high-impact sites (face, hands, genitals, scalp) and quality of life.
**Screen for psoriatic arthritis** every year with the PEST questionnaire, especially in the first 10 years.
**Tests are rarely needed.** Biopsy if uncertain. Take a throat swab if guttate psoriasis follows a recent sore throat.
**Comorbidities:** assess cardiovascular risk (NICE: at presentation, and at least every 5 years if severe), lifestyle and mood.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Greasier scale on the central face; can overlap (‘sebopsoriasis’)
Asymmetrical with an advancing edge; mycology positive
Violaceous, flat-topped papules with Wickham striae; wrists and mucosa
Coin-shaped, very itchy, often on the legs
Satellite papules and pustules, macerated; flexural psoriasis is sharply defined with no satellites

management: Aligned with **NICE CG153** and the CKS summary.

list: Use emollients regularly. They reduce scale and itch and help active topicals work.
Lifestyle: weight loss if overweight, stopping smoking, moderating alcohol, and support with stress.
Seek review promptly for unexplained joint pain or swelling.

ol: **Potent steroid once daily plus vitamin D analogue once daily**, applied at different times of day, for up to 4 weeks.
If not controlled: **vitamin D analogue twice daily** for 8–12 weeks.
Then either a potent steroid twice daily (short course) or coal tar, **or** fixed-combination **calcipotriol/betamethasone** once daily for up to 4 weeks, which helps adherence.
Plan a **4-week break** between courses of potent or very potent steroid, using a non-steroid topical in between.
Do not exceed the maximum durations: potent steroid **≤ 8 weeks** per site; very potent **≤ 4 weeks**, usually on specialist advice.

management: Start with a **potent steroid** in a suitable formulation (lotion, gel or shampoo). Next steps are calcipotriol/betamethasone combination or a vitamin D analogue. Use scale softeners (e.g. salicylic acid) for thick scale. Coal tar shampoo alone is not enough for severe scalp disease.
Use a **mild to moderate** steroid short term (up to about 2 weeks). **Do not** use potent or very potent steroids here. Experienced clinicians may use calcineurin inhibitors to spare steroids.
NICE recommends **specialist referral at presentation**. Primary care options are limited by age and licensing.

Methotrexate (often the first conventional option), ciclosporin (for rapid control or when planning conception) and acitretin, followed by biologics or TYK2 inhibitors under NICE technology appraisals.
red_flags: **Erythroderma** (widespread redness over 90% of the skin) or **generalised pustular psoriasis**: same-day dermatology or hospital assessment.
Suspected **psoriatic arthritis** (swollen or painful joints, dactylitis, enthesitis): refer to rheumatology.
BSA over 10%, moderate or worse severity, failure of topicals, or a major impact on quality of life: refer for phototherapy or systemics.
Severe nail disease, children, and diagnostic uncertainty: refer.
pearls: Explain that psoriasis is **chronic** and treatment is intermittent. Most patients relapse after stopping.
Demonstrate how to apply treatment. Cosmetic acceptability drives adherence, so gels and foams often beat ointments for daytime use.
Spell out **steroid breaks** to prevent atrophy and rebound.
Calcipotriol/betamethasone combinations (Dovobet®-type gel, foam or ointment) vary by formulary, so check local brands.
**Avoid oral steroids.** Withdrawal can trigger rebound or pustular flares.
Counsel on vaccination and infection risk if the patient later moves to immunosuppression (specialist-led).
NICE notes a higher VTE risk in severe psoriasis, so keep it in mind.
